deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 86 is a page of German-language notes on Greek history, the 5th century BC, apparently from a lecture course. It continues the previous page, which covers Pericles, Tanagra (457) and the five-year truce of 451. The next page continues with 'Lage von Griechenland, vor diesem Kriege' (the situation of Greece before the war). Marginal dates 450, 449 and 445 appear on the left; a pencil folio number 86 and an old page number '7-4' (or '4') appear at top.

Content, paragraph by paragraph:

(1) Cimon's plan was to renew the war against Persia.
- 450: he received command of a powerful fleet, sailed against the Persians and defeated their fleet and land army.
- He then sailed against Cyprus (my reading of 'Er segelte darauf gegen Cyprus').
- 449: Persia's precarious situation ('die damalige mißliche Lage') brought Artaxerxes to make peace under very humiliating conditions. This is the so-called Peace of Callias.
- Cimon died (marked with a dagger, †) before the peace was concluded, 'too early for Athens'. Pericles thereafter stood alone at the head of the state ('an der Spitze').

(2) Pericles had a large party against him but maintained his position. He gave the Athenians the feeling that the city had risen through him.
- Meanwhile the five-year truce ended, and the Peloponnesians seemed about to break the peace again.
- 445: hence a peace for 30 years was concluded (the Thirty Years' Peace), which lasted only 14 years.
- These years of peace were nonetheless restless. A ferment arose across Greece, and the jealousy between Athens and Sparta grew daily, so that small occasions sufficed. The marginal note gives an example: 'z.B. im Kriege der Corinther gegen Corcyra'.
- The Athenians sent a fleet to support the Corcyraeans. The Corinthians turned to Sparta, 'and so arose the Peloponnesian War'.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct. The only numerical content is chronological: 451 + 5 = 446 for the end of the truce, and 445 + 14 = 431 for the outbreak of the war. Both agree with the next page's '431 ... der 27 jährige Krieg'.

The filing under 'HB.Lagrange1816' looks like a cataloguing or binding accident. The page may be lecture notes, possibly from Gauss's student years or by another hand, bound with mathematical material. Authorship is not something I can settle from this page alone.
errors: No mathematical errors; there is no mathematics on the page.

Historical content matches the standard chronology of the time: Cimon's Cyprus expedition and death c. 450/449, Peace of Callias 449, Thirty Years' Peace 446/445, Peloponnesian War from 431. Modern scholars debate whether the Peace of Callias really happened and on what terms; the note presents it uncritically.
Minor: the 30-year peace is usually dated 446/445; 445 + 14 = 431 is consistent with the stated 14 years.
The final sentence is garbled: 'an Sparta' appears twice, once probably as a leftover from a reworded phrase.

results.what: Narrative history of Athens c. 450–431 BC: Cimon's last campaign, the Peace of Callias, Pericles' ascendancy, the Thirty Years' Peace, the Corcyra affair and the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War
results.usually_credited_to: Thucydides (primary source); standard 18th/19th-century textbook and lecture material (e.g. Göttingen history lectures)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is non-mathematical historical lecture notes on standard Greek history; nothing here bears on mathematics or on Gauss's scientific priority.

checkable.asserts: The five-year truce of 451 BC expires around 446 BC, just before the 30-year peace dated 445 on the page.
A peace concluded in 445 BC that lasted 14 years ends in 431 BC, the outbreak of the Peloponnesian War given on the next page.
The '27 jährige Krieg' (27-year war) of the next page ends in 404 BC, consistent with the standard dating.

transcription_corrections: Line 4–5: '...und sie schlug, Flotte und Landarmee' – the Persian fleet and land army were defeated.
'Er erhielte[?] dadurch gegen Cyprus' should probably read 'Er segelte darauf gegen Cyprus'.

'und die damalige ... Lage' should read 'und die damalige mißliche Lage, brachte Artaxerxes dahin, Friede zu machen, unter sehr demüthigenden Bedingungen'. 'unter' is struck and rewritten; 'demüthigen den' should be 'demüthigenden'.

'Cimon + ... kam, leider zu früh für Athen, wiederstand zu Friede' should read 'Cimon † (starb) ehe der Friede zu Stande kam, leider zu früh für Athen, wodurch Peri-kles jetzt allein [an der] Spitze stand'. 'Spitze' is an insertion at line end, and 'kles' (misread as 'Perikles[?]') begins the next line.
'das Gefühl zu erstellen[?], daß ... durch ihn gestiegen' should probably read 'daß sie durch ihn gestiegen [seien]'.
'Antworts[?] ... der 5 jährige Friede' should read 'Unterdessen endigte sich der 5 jährige Friede'.
'wieder ... brechen zu wollen' should read 'wieder auf[zu]brechen zu wollen' or 'wieder aus[zu]brechen'.
'daher brauchte diese nur kleine Gelegenheiten wie' is closer to 'nur kleiner Gelegenheiten' followed by the † reference mark to the marginal note.
'eine Flotte daher als Hülfe ab' should read 'eine Flotte dahin als Hülfe ab'.
Margin: 'z.B. im Kriege der Corinther gegen Corcyra.' – the transcription is correct.
Page number at top: '7-4' is likely a struck '7' followed by '4', or an old gathering mark; the pencil '86' is the folio number.
